title: 1 Kings 21:17–29
context: The LORD sends Elijah to confront Ahab in Naboth’s vineyard with judgment on Ahab, his house, and Jezebel. When Ahab humbles himself, the LORD delays the disaster until his son’s days.

verses.text: The LORD’s word came to Elijah the Tishbite, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: “The LORD’s word came to Elijah the Tishbite.” Arminian readers see God refusing to let injustice against an ordinary Israelite go unanswered.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s word breaking in at the very moment Ahab takes the vineyard. Readers in this tradition stress that God sees the crime that human courts approved.

verses.text: “Arise, go down to meet Ahab king of Israel, who dwells in Samaria. Behold, he is in the vineyard of Naboth, where he has gone down to take possession of it.
verses.arminianNotes: God tells Elijah, “Behold, he is in the vineyard of Naboth, where he has gone down to take possession of it.” Arminian readers see God holding Ahab directly accountable.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s knowledge of Ahab’s actions. The instruction sends the prophet to confront the king at the scene of the injustice.

verses.text: You shall speak to him, saying, ‘The LORD says, “Have you killed and also taken possession?” ’ You shall speak to him, saying, ‘The LORD says, “In the place where dogs licked the blood of Naboth, dogs will lick your blood, even yours.” ’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: Elijah is to say, “Have you killed and also taken possession?” and “dogs will lick your blood, even yours.” Arminian readers see judgment matching the crime, stated soberly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s just sentence. Readers in this tradition note that 1 Kings 22:38 and 2 Kings 9:25–26 relate to this word, and interpreters discuss how the details correspond without agreeing on one account.

verses.text: Ahab said to Elijah, “Have you found me, my enemy?” He answered, “I have found you, because you have sold yourself to do that which is evil in the LORD’s sight.
verses.arminianNotes: Ahab says, “Have you found me, my enemy?” Elijah answers, “I have found you, because you have sold yourself to do that which is evil in the LORD’s sight.” Arminian readers see Ahab responsible for his chosen path.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Ahab’s guilt named plainly. The phrase “sold yourself” portrays deliberate commitment to evil, not accidental wrongdoing.

verses.text: Behold, I will bring evil on you, and will utterly sweep you away and will cut off from Ahab everyone who urinates against a wall, and him who is shut up and him who is left at large in Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: God declares, “I will bring evil on you, and will utterly sweep you away.” Arminian readers see judgment on a dynasty that persisted in evil.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s judgment on Ahab’s house. The engwebp footnote gives “male” as an alternative rendering for the idiom about urination; it is a translation note.

verses.text: I will make your house like the house of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, and like the house of Baasha the son of Ahijah, for the provocation with which you have provoked me to anger, and have made Israel to sin.”
verses.arminianNotes: “I will make your house like the house of Jeroboam … and like the house of Baasha.” Arminian readers see God holding dynasties accountable for leading Israel into sin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the pattern of judgment on unfaithful dynasties in 1 Kings 15 and 16. The charge that Ahab “made Israel to sin” highlights his responsibility as king.

verses.text: The LORD also spoke of Jezebel, saying, “The dogs will eat Jezebel by the rampart of Jezreel.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “The dogs will eat Jezebel by the rampart of Jezreel.” Arminian readers see Jezebel held personally accountable for orchestrating Naboth’s murder.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s judgment on Jezebel for her central role. The sentence is stated soberly, and its fulfillment is recorded in 2 Kings 9:30–37.

verses.text: The dogs will eat whoever dies of Ahab in the city; and the birds of the sky will eat whoever dies in the field.”
verses.arminianNotes: “The dogs will eat whoever dies of Ahab in the city; and the birds of the sky will eat whoever dies in the field.” Arminian readers see the disgrace of an unburied death as part of the judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a sobering word about the end of Ahab’s line. The language reflects the shame of lacking burial, a theme found in other prophetic judgments.

verses.text: But there was no one like Ahab, who sold himself to do that which was evil in the LORD’s sight, whom Jezebel his wife stirred up.
verses.arminianNotes: The narrator says “… there was no one like Ahab, who sold himself to do that which was evil … whom Jezebel his wife stirred up.” Arminian readers see Ahab responsible for his evil, though encouraged by Jezebel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see both Ahab and Jezebel named in the narrator’s verdict. Jezebel’s influence does not lessen Ahab’s guilt, and readers in this tradition stress that both bear responsibility.

verses.text: He did very abominably in following idols, according to all that the Amorites did, whom the LORD cast out before the children of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: Ahab “did very abominably in following idols, according to all that the Amorites did.” Arminian readers see Ahab adopting the practices of the nations God had driven out.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the gravity of Ahab’s idolatry. The comparison with the Amorites underlines how far Israel’s king had departed from God’s covenant.

verses.text: When Ahab heard those words, he tore his clothes, put sackcloth on his body, fasted, lay in sackcloth, and went about despondently.
verses.arminianNotes: Ahab tears his clothes, puts on sackcloth, fasts, and goes about despondently. Arminian readers see a real humbling before God after hearing the word of judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Ahab humbling himself, as God himself acknowledges in verse 29. Readers in this tradition generally avoid speculating about Ahab’s inner state beyond what God says about it.

verses.text: The LORD’s word came to Elijah the Tishbite, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: “The LORD’s word came to Elijah the Tishbite.” Arminian readers see God responding to Ahab’s humbling, showing his readiness to show mercy even to a wicked king.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God speaking again through his prophet. The repetition of the formula from verse 17 signals a new word that modifies the timing of the judgment.

verses.text: “See how Ahab humbles himself before me? Because he humbles himself before me, I will not bring the evil in his days; but I will bring the evil on his house in his son’s day.”
verses.arminianNotes: God says, “Because he humbles himself before me, I will not bring the evil in his days; but I will bring the evil on his house in his son’s day.” Arminian readers see God’s real response to Ahab’s humbling; the Jonah 3:10 box treats this question.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see judgment delayed, not canceled. Readers in this tradition relate God’s timing to his sovereign purpose, as the Genesis 15:16 box discusses, and treat the delay as shared ground on God’s patience.
